newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronists vow to battle courts on labor reform.
newsitem.headline: Peronists vow to battle courts on labor reform.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem's Peronist government promised Tuesday to fight court objections to his decrees on labor reforms, declared unconstitutional by one judge and frozen by another.

Menem, struggling to implement reforms he considers vital to fighting a 17.3 percent unemployment rate, has threatened to seek the impeachment of a judge who challenged his decrees 10 days ago. His Chief of Staff Alberto Kohan made the same threat against the judge who ordered them suspended Monday.
"I think the government has the right to seek impeachment when there are unfounded rulings," Kohan told local radio.

President Menem's brother Eduardo, a Peronist senator, said the government's main problem was with 77-year-old Labor Judge Julio Garcia Martinez who declared the decrees ordered by Menem in late December unconstitutional.

Sen. Menem promised the government would comply with the ruling Monday of Labor Judge Ines Gassibe Monday suspending the decrees pending an explanation by the government. She was acting on a petition by the main CGT trade union federation.
"The government will appeal the absolutely illegitimate ruling of Garcia Martinez and reply to questions from the judge in the other case," Eduardo Menem told local radio.

"If the courts decide that it cannot be done by decree, the government will respect those rulings," he said, taking a more conciliatory tone than other government officials who slammed Garcia Martinez's ruling as "political".

Menem resorted to decrees in the face of opposition in Congress and a breakdown in negotiations with unions, who fear their power is under threat. The CGT staged a 24-hour general strike on December 26, its third in the year.

His Peronist government had been working on another batch of decrees to follow up the first three, which allow workers to choose their union health plan, let smaller firms bypass national unions in collective pay talks and let firms appeal to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis.

CGT press chief Carlos West Ocampo called the attempt to rule by decree a sign of "impotence founded on incompetence." The union campaign was reinforced Tuesday by the hardline MTA union faction's decision not to carry out its threat to break with the CGT -- as long as the labor reform fight continues.
